title: Get a Linux you can break
objective: By the end of this lesson you have a working Linux terminal in front of you, on a machine where breaking things costs you nothing.

blocks.text: You cannot learn this by reading. You need a machine you are willing to destroy, because the fastest way to understand what a command does is to run it somewhere the consequences are free.
Pick whichever of these matches the computer in front of you. All three give you a real Linux command line.
Windows Subsystem for Linux runs a real Linux kernel alongside Windows. It is the least friction of any option and it is what most people should use.

blocks.caption: In PowerShell, as administrator
lines: # then restart, and open "Ubuntu" from the Start menu

blocks.text: On macOS: a virtual machine, not the built-in terminal

macOS gives you a Unix terminal, which feels similar and will get you through the early lessons. But it is not Linux — some commands differ, and the permission and package sections later will not match. Install a free virtualisation tool and run Ubuntu inside it.
On anything, including a tablet: a cloud shell

Every major cloud provider offers a free browser-based Linux shell attached to your account. Nothing to install. The trade-off is that these sessions reset, so treat anything you save there as temporary.

blocks.title: Do not practise on something that matters
blocks.text: Never learn these commands on a machine that holds work data, or on a server anyone depends on. Part of the point is to make mistakes. Make them where the worst outcome is rebuilding a throwaway machine.
You now have a black window with a prompt in it. The prompt usually ends in $ and is the system waiting for you to type. Three commands will confirm everything is wired up.

blocks.title: Your first three commands
blocks.expected: A username, then a path that probably starts with /home, then a long line naming the kernel. If all three answered, your environment is ready for the rest of the course.

blocks.title: Two habits worth forming now
blocks.text: Press Tab to complete a half-typed name instead of typing it out — it prevents typos in exactly the places typos are expensive. Press the up arrow to bring back the previous command instead of retyping it.

cheatsheet: macOS: run Ubuntu in a VM — the built-in terminal is Unix but not Linux
Anywhere: a provider's browser cloud shell, but treat storage as temporary
Never practise on a machine holding real data
whoami = which user · pwd = where am I · uname -a = what system is this
Tab completes names · up arrow recalls the last command

checkpoint.prompt: You are on Windows and want the lowest-friction real Linux environment. What do you use?

choices.C: The Windows command prompt, which is the same thing
choices.D: A remote desktop into a colleague's machine

checkpoint.explanation: WSL runs a real Linux kernel next to Windows. The Windows command prompt is a different system with different commands entirely.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is the macOS terminal not a perfect substitute for Linux in this course?

choices.A: It is Unix-like and feels similar, but some commands and the package and permission behaviour differ from Linux
choices.B: It cannot run any of the commands in this course
choices.C: It has no command line at all

checkpoint.explanation: It will carry you through the early navigation lessons, then diverge exactly where the course gets specific — package management and some permission details.

checkpoint.prompt: Which command answers "where am I in the filesystem right now?"
checkpoint.explanation: pwd prints the working directory. whoami answers who, uname answers what system, and ls lists what is here — a different question.
